reasoning: Both outputs refuse to write a PRD, interrogate the solution-shaped request, and end at 3/10 PRD readiness with an explicit blocker list — so on the headline behaviour they are equivalent. B wins on three margins. (1) It answers the actual question structurally: section 3, 'What would have to be true for this to be worth building', is a five-row falsifiable table with a 'cheapest check' and a 'Unknown — blocking' status per row, three of which are one query away. A covers the same ground but scatters it across a break-even formula, a risk list and a closing blocking-questions list, so the reader has to assemble it. (2) B's factual claims are tighter and better sourced: it cites Google's own sender-guidelines page for the 0.3%/0.1% thresholds and dates Microsoft's rejection policy precisely (5 May 2025, dmarcian), and it appends an explicit caveat that vendor benchmark figures are not comparable to the user's baseline. A sources the same territory to SEO-style blogs (PowerDMARC, MailOver, reactemailspro) and asserts a broad 'since November 2025 non-compliant mail is rejected outright' claim that generalises one provider's policy across all of them — A itself walks back the deliverability framing in its Stress Test as scale-dependent. (3) B is cheaper to act on: it offers a two-hour fake-door checkbox pre-probe below the three-week concierge probe, a concrete subdomain-isolation mitigation, a branch table for 'what happens next', and closes on a precise ask — three numbers. A's counter-strengths are real and nearly close the gap: the J1/J2/J3 split ('three features wearing one name') is the single sharpest analytical move in either document, and its Option B reframe — batch the per-event emails you already send, so the feature *reduces* email volume instead of adding to it — is a genuinely valuable idea B never reaches. But A pays for that breadth: it commits to a headline recommendation (build J3) that its own Stress Test concedes is the least-evidenced claim in the document, and it carries material the user did not ask for (a tentative phased roadmap, a table of 'my unverified prior' on competitors, and a five-item appendix about improving the skill itself). For a user whose entire question is 'is this worth building', B's tighter signal-to-noise and its explicit what-must-be-true ledger serve the decision better.
